How Great Leaders Inspire Action | Simon Sinek | TED signal 1
TED · 18:35 · 22,200,330 views · Watch ↗
Read transcript · ~3,462 words

Translator: Mislav Ante Omazić - EFZG Reviewer: Predrag Pale How can you explain when things don't go the way we assumed? Or better yet, how can you explain when others are able to accomplish things that defy all assumptions? For example: Why is Apple so innovative? Year after year, year after year, they are more innovative than their competitors. And yet, they are just a computer company. They are like everyone else. They have the same access to the same talent, the same agencies, the same consultants, the same media. So why do they seem so different? Why did Martin Luther King lead the Civil Rights Movement?

He was not the only one who suffered from the lack of civil rights in America. And he was certainly not the only great orator of the time. Why him? And why exactly were the Wirght brothers able to understand controlled flight with an engine when there were other teams that had better qualifications, more resources and they did not make the first flight, and the Wright brothers beat them. Something else was important here. About three and a half years ago I came to a realization, and that realization profoundly changed my perspective on the way the world works. It has even profoundly changed the way I do business.

As it turns out -- there is a pattern -- as it turns out, all the great and inspiring leaders and organizations around the world, whether it's Apple, or Martin Luther King, or the Wright brothers, they all thought, behaved, and communicated in exactly the same way. And that's in a completely different way than all the others. All I did was codify it. And that's probably the simplest idea in the world. I call it the golden circle. Why? How? What? That little idea explains why some organizations and some leaders can inspire others, while others cannot. Let me quickly define the key elements. Every person, every organization on the Planet knows what they are doing, 100%.

Some know how to do it, whether you call it your value proposition or your own process or unique selling proposition. But very, very few people or organizations know why they do what they do. And by "why" I don't mean the way "they make a profit". That's the result. That is always the result. By "why" I mean: what is your purpose? What is your calling, meaning? What do you believe in? Why does your organization exist? Why do you get out of bed every morning? And why should anyone care? As a result, the way we think, the way we act, the way we communicate is from the outside in. That's obvious.

Let's go from the most obvious to the most complicated thing. Whereas inspirational leaders and inspiring organizations, regardless of their size, regardless of what they do, all think, act and communicate from the inside out . Let me give you an example. I use Apple because they are easy to understand and anyone can do it. If Apple were like everyone else, their marketing message would be. "We make great computers. They are beautifully designed, easy to use, and user-friendly. Would you like to buy one?" Nope. And that's how most of us communicate. That's how most marketing is done. That's how most sales are done.

And that's how most of us communicate with other people. We say what we do, we say how we are different or how we are better and we expect some form of behavior, a purchase, a vote, something like that. Here is our new law office. We have the best lawyers and the biggest clients. We always do the work for our clients. Here is our new car. He is very frugal. It has leather seats. Buy our car. But it is uninspiring. Here's how Apple really communicates. "Everything we do, we believe in changing the status quo. We believe in a different way of thinking. The way we provoke the status quo is by making our products beautifully designed, easy to use, and customer-centric.

We just happen to make great computers. Would you like to buy one?" Completely different, right? Are you ready to buy a computer from me? All I did was reverse the order of the information. What we've learned is that people don't buy what you do; people buy why you do it. People don't buy what you do; they buy why you do it. This explains why every person in this hall is perfectly happy to buy a computer from Apple. But we feel perfectly comfortable buying an MP3 player from Apple, or a cell phone from Apple, or a digital video recorder from Apple. But, as I said earlier, Apple is just a computer company.

There is nothing that distinguishes them structurally from any of their competitors. Their competitors are equally qualified to make all of these products. In fact, they tried to do that. A few years ago, Gateway came to market with a flat-screen television. They are famously qualified to make flat-screen TVs. They've been making flat screens for their monitors for years. Nobody bought one. Dell came out with MP3 players and PDAs. And they made a great quality product. And they are capable of making a well-designed product. Nobody bought any of them. In fact, as I'm talking about it now, we can't even imagine buying an MP3 player from Dell.

Why would you buy an MP3 player from a computer company? But we do it almost every day. People don't buy what you do; they buy why you do it. The goal is not to do business with everyone who needs what you have. The goal is to do business with people who believe in what you believe in. Here's the best part. None of what I'm telling you is my opinion. Everything is based on the principles of biology. Not psychology, biology. If you look at a cross-section of the human brain, looking from top to bottom, what you see is that the human brain is actually made up of three main units that perfectly match the golden circle.

Our newest brain, our homo sapiens brain, our neocortex, overlaps with the "what" level. The neocortex is responsible for all our rational and analytical thinking and language. The middle two sections make up our limbic system. And our limbic system is responsible for all our feelings, like trust and loyalty. It is also responsible for human behavior, all decision-making, and has no capacity for language. In other words, when we communicate from the outside in, yes, people can understand large amounts of complicated information like features, benefits, facts, and numbers. It simply does not affect behavior.

When we can communicate from the inside out, we speak directly to the part of the brain that controls behavior, and then we allow people to rationalize it to themselves with tangible things we say and do. This is where intuitive decisions come from. You know, sometimes you can give someone all the facts and figures, and they say, "I know what all the numbers and details are telling us, but it just doesn't seem right." Why would we use that verb, we don't "feel" good? Because the part of our brain that controls decision-making doesn't control language. And the best we can say is, "I don't know.

It just doesn't seem good." Either you simply say you are heart-led, or you are soul-led. I hate to tell you this, but it's not your body parts that control your behavior. It all happens here in your limbic system, the part of the brain that controls decision-making, but not language. But if you don't know why you do what you do, and people respond to why you do what you do, then how are you ever going to get people to vote for you, to buy something from you, or, more importantly, to be loyal and want to be a part of what you do. Again, the goal isn't just to sell to people who need what you have; The goal is to sell to people who believe what you believe.

The goal is not just to employ people who need work; The goal is to hire people who believe what you believe. I always say, you know, if you hire people just because they can do the job, then they'll only work for the money, but if you hire people who believe in what you believe in, they'll work for you with blood, sweat, and tears. And there is no better example of this than that of the Wright brothers. Most people don't know who Samuel Pierpont Langley is. In the early 20th century, the search for a powered aircraft was something like the dot.com of today. Everyone tried. And Samuel Pierpont Langley had, what we would think, a recipe for success.

I mean, even now, if you were to ask people, "Why did your product or your company fail?" people will always give you some variation of the same answer, the same three things, lack of capital, the wrong people, bad market conditions. Always the same three things, which we will now explore. Samuel Pierpont Langley received US$50,000 from the War Department to build this flying machine. Money was not a problem. He had his own place at Harvard and worked at the Smithsonian Institute, and was very well-connected. He knew all the great minds of the time. He hired the best minds money could find. And the market conditions were fantastic.

The New York Times followed him everywhere. And everyone was rooting for Langley. Then how come you've never heard of Samuel Pierpont Langley? A few hundred miles away in Dayton, Ohio, Orville and Wilbur Wright had none of what we consider a recipe for success. They had no money. They paid for their dream with the money they earned at the bicycle shop. Not a single person on the Wright brothers' team had a college degree, not even Orville or Wilbur. And the New York Times didn't follow them anywhere. The difference was that Orville and Wilbur were driven by purpose, by calling, by meaning, by conviction.

They believed that if they could build this flying machine, it would change the course of the world. Samuel Pierpont Langley was different. He wanted to be rich, and he wanted to be famous. He was chasing results. He was on the hunt for wealth. And look what happened. People who believed in the Wright Brothers' dream worked with them with blood, sweat, and tears. Others worked only for pay. And they told stories about how the Wright brothers would take five sets of parts every time they went out, because that's the number of times they would crash before they got to dinner. Then, finally, on December 17, 1903, the Wright brothers took flight, and no one was there to witness it.

We found out about it a few days later. And further proof that Langley was motivated by the wrong things was the fact that on the day the Wright brothers took flight, he quit his job. He could have said, "That's an incredible discovery, guys, and I'm going to advance your technology," but he didn't. He was n't the first, he didn't get rich, he did n't become famous, so he gave up. People don't buy what you do; they buy why you do it. And if you say what you believe, you will attract those who believe what you believe. But why is it important to attract those who believe what you believe? Something called the law of diffusion of innovation.

And if you don't know the law itself, you certainly know the terminology. The top 2.5% of our population are our innovators. The next 13.5% of our population are the first to adopt innovation. The next 34% are the early majority, 34% the late majority and 16% those who are lagging behind. The only reason these people buy push-button phones is because they can't buy the classic rotary dial ones anymore. (Laughter) We all find ourselves at different places at different times on that scale, but what the law of diffusion of innovation tells us is that if you want mass market success or mass market adoption of an idea, you can't achieve that unless you reach that critical tipping point between 15 and 18% market penetration, and then the system takes over.

And I like to ask business people, "What is the stage of your transition to a new job?" And they like to proudly answer me, "Oh, it's about 10%." Okay, you can easily stumble upon 10% of customers. We all have that 10% who just "get it". That's how we describe them, right? It's like that intuition, "Oh, they just get it." The problem is: How do you find those who understand before you start working with them versus those who don't? So it's this here, this little gap, that you have to close, as Jeffrey Moore calls it, "cross the chasm." Because, you see, the early majority won't try something until someone else has tried it first.

And these people, the innovators and the early adopters, they casually make such instinctive decisions. They make intuitive decisions much more easily, guided by their understanding of the world, not just the products that are available. These are the people who stood in line for 6 hours to buy an iPhone when it first came out, while others simply walked into a store a week later and bought the same device off the shelf. These are the people who paid US$40,000 for a flat-screen TV when it first came out, even though the technology was substandard. And, by the way, they didn't do it because the technology was so great.

They did it for themselves. Because they wanted to be first. People don't buy what you do; they buy why you do it. And what you do simply proves what you believe. In fact, people will do things to prove what they believe. The reason why that person bought the iPhone in the first 6 hours, why they stood in line for 6 hours, is because that's how they perceive the world, and that's how they want others to see them. They were the first. People don't buy what you do; they buy why you do it. Let me give you a perfect example, the glorious failure and glorious success of the Law of Innovation Diffusion.

First, a glorious failure. That's a commercial example. As we said earlier, a few seconds ago, the recipe for success is money, the right people, and the right market conditions. Exactly. If you have that, then success is guaranteed. Look at TiVo. From the time TiVo came on the market, 8 or 9 years ago, to this day, they have been the only such product of the highest quality on the market, hats off, there is no debate about that. They were extremely well funded. Market conditions were fantastic. I mean, we use TiVo as a verb. I TiVo stuff on that piece of Time Warner DVR junk all the time. But TiVo is a commercial failure.

They never made any money. And when they started their initial public offering, their stock was about US$30-40 to sink, and it never got back above 10. In fact, I don't think it ever went above 6, except for a few brief occasions. Because you see, when TiVo released their product, they told us everything they had. They said, "We have a product that will pause live TV, skip commercials, rewind live TV, and memorize your viewing habits without you asking it." And the cynical majority said, "We don't trust you. We don't need it. We don't like it. You're scaring us." What if they said, "If you're the type of person who likes to have complete control over every aspect of your life, man, what a product we have for you.

It pauses live streams, skips promos, memorizes your viewing habits, etc., etc." People don't buy what you do; they buy why you do it. And what you do simply serves as proof of what you believe. Now I will give you a successful example of the law of diffusion of innovation. In the summer of 1963, 250,000 people showed up at a shopping mall in Washington to hear Dr. King speak. No one sent out invitations, and there was no website to check the date. How do you do that? Dr. King wasn't the only man in America who was a good speaker. He was not the only man in America who suffered for civil rights in America.

In fact, some of his ideas were bad. But he had a gift. He didn't go around telling people what needed to change in America. He went around telling people what he believed. "I believe. I believe. I believe," he told the people. And people who believed in what he believed took up his call and made it their own, and told others about it. And some of these people created structures to spread the word to even more people. And lo and behold, 250,000 people showed up on the right day, at the right time, to hear him speak. How many of them showed up because of him? Zero. They showed up for themselves.

It was because of what they believed about America that they traveled eight hours, to stand in the sun in Washington in the middle of August. It was because of what they believed in and not because of black versus white. 25% of the viewers were white. Dr. King believed that there were two kinds of laws in the world, those made by a higher authority and those made by people. And until all laws made by men are consistent with laws made by a higher authority, we will not live in a just world. It so happened that the Civil Rights Movement was the perfect thing to help him achieve his purpose. We followed, not for him, but for ourselves.

And , along the way, he gave us the "I have a dream" speech, not the "I have a plan" speech. (Laughter) Listen to the politicians now with their 12-point general plans. They don't inspire anyone. Because there are leaders and those who lead. Leaders hold a position of power or authority. However, those who lead inspire us. Whether it's individuals or organizations, we follow those who lead, not because we have to, but because we want to. We follow those who lead, not for their sake, but for our own. Those who start with "why" have the ability to inspire those around them or find others who will inspire them.

Thank you very much. (Applause)

They are more likely to make intuitive decisions that are guided by their beliefs about the world and not simply by the qualities of the product. These are the people who stood in line for 6 hours to buy an iPhone when it first came out. Or they could just go next week and not wait. These are the people who spent $40,000 on a flat screen TV when it first came out, even though the technology was substandard. They didn't do it because the technology is great, but for their own sake. Because they wanted to be first. People don't buy what you do, they buy the reason you do it. What you do is only proof of what you believe.

People actually do the things that prove their beliefs. The reason you buy an iPhone in the first 6 hours, standing in line for 6 hours, is related to your beliefs about the world and how you want others to see you: They were first. People don't buy what you do, they buy the reason you do it. Let me give you a famous example, a famous failure and a famous success of the law of diffusion of innovation. First the famous failure. The example is commercial. As we said a moment ago, the recipe for success is money, the right people, and the right market conditions. Right? Then you must be successful.

Look at TiVo. From the moment TiVo came out 8-9 years ago until today, they remain the highest quality product on the market, there is no dispute about that. They were very well funded. Market conditions were fantastic. We even use TiVo as a verb. I "tweet" cable shows all the time. But TiVo was a commercial failure. They failed to make any money. When they went public, their shares were $30-40, and then they fell and never rose above $10. I don't even think they trade above $6, except for some brief spikes. When TiVo launched their product, they told us about its features. They said, "We have a product that pauses the TV, skips commercials, skips parts of the show, and remembers your preferences without you even asking." And the cynical majority said, "We don't believe you.

We don't need this. We don't like it. You're scaring us." What if they had said: "If you're someone who likes to have complete control over every aspect of your life, then this product is for you. It pauses live broadcasts, skips commercials, remembers your preferences, etc." People don't buy what you do, they buy the reason you do it. What you do only serves to prove your beliefs. Let me now give you a successful example of the law of diffusion of innovation. In the summer of 1963, 250,000 people came to the park in Washington to hear Dr. King speak. There were no invitations sent out, no website to check the date.

How did they do it? Dr. King was not the only great orator in America. He was not the only person suffering from a lack of rights. In fact, some of his ideas were not good. But he had a gift. He didn't go around preaching what needed to change in America. He traveled around and spoke about what he believed in. "I believe, I believe, I believe," he said. And people who believed the same thing adopted his cause as their own and passed it on to others. Some of these people created structures to reach even more people. And look, 250,000 people came on the right day, at the right time, to hear him speak.

How many of them went there because of him? Zero. They have gone for themselves. Their beliefs about America led them to travel 8 hours by bus and stand under the sun in Washington in the middle of August. Because of their beliefs, and not just blacks versus whites: 25% of the audience was white. Dr. King believed that there were two types of laws in the world: those made by a higher authority and those made by people. And only when the laws made by people correspond to the laws made by a higher authority will we live in a just world. And so it happened that the Civil Rights Movement became the ideal channel for pursuing his cause.

We followed him, not for him, but for ourselves. And by the way, his speech begins with "I have a dream," not "I have a plan." (laughter) Listen to the politicians today with their 12-point plans. They don't inspire anyone. Because there are leaders and there are those who lead. Leaders have a position of power or authority, but those who lead inspire us. Whether they are people or organizations, we follow those who lead, not because we have to, but because we want to. We follow those who lead, not for their sake, but for ourselves. People who start with the question "Why" have the ability to inspire those around them or find others who do.

Thank you very much.

Translator: Sophia Kuchina Editor: Natalia Ost I am very glad to be here. You have the power to change the world. I don't want this to sound cliche, but you really can do it. Deep within you, each of you, is the most powerful instrument known to humanity. This tool is an idea. So, one idea in our minds can make a revolution, start a new movement, and it has real power to change our future. But an idea is powerless if it remains inside you. If this idea remains with you, inaccessible to others, it will die with you. Maybe some of you tried to pitch your idea but it was not accepted, it was rejected and some other mediocre idea was approved.

And the only difference between them was how they were presented. Because if you express an idea in a way that resonates, change will happen and you can change the world. My family collects vintage European posters. Every time we go to Maui, we go to a local vendor and he puts out these awesome posters. I love them. Each one has one idea and one single image that conveys it. They are the size of a mattress - very large. Not as dense as a mattress, but they are large. The seller will tell you the story by turning the pages. At that time, I had my two children next to me, and he turns the page, and at the bottom is this poster.

And at that moment, I leaned forward and said, “Oh my God! "How I love this poster!" — the children jumped back and exclaimed: “Oh my God! "Mom, it's you!" And here is this poster. (Laughter) See, it's like I'm saying, "Fire!" I liked the irony in this poster. Here's this beauty, all ready for battle, like a standard bearer, and she's holding these little baking spices like they're nothing, even though she's willing to give her life to advertise them. So if you replace those little baking spices with presentation... Yeah, I'm that excited. I was inspired by performing before it was considered cool.

I truly believe they have the power to change the world if used effectively to communicate an idea. Changing the world is not easy. This won't happen if there is only one person with one idea. The idea must spread or it will have no effect. Therefore, it must come from you and be accessible to others. The most effective way to convey an idea is to tell a story. For thousands of years, illiterate people have been passing on their values ​​and culture to their descendants, intact and safe, from generation to generation. So there is something magical about the structure of a story that, once it is told, makes it easy for the listener to absorb and remember it.

In general, a story being told evokes a physical reaction: your heart may beat faster, your eyes may widen, you may say, “Oh, I get goosebumps” or “I feel a little sick in the pit of my stomach. ” We react physically when someone tells us a story. So even if the scene doesn't change, you can tell a story, but the performance will be a complete failure. And I wanted to understand why. Why is it that we sit spellbound when listening to a story, but the same doesn't happen with a performance. So I wanted to understand how I could incorporate stories into my performances. We had thousands of presentations in that store, hundreds of thousands in fact.

So I knew cases of really bad presentations. I decided to start by studying film and literature, to really delve into the subject and understand what was going on and why it didn't work that way. So, I want to show you some of my findings, which, as I found out, led to a specific form of performance. The obvious step was to start with Aristotle. He believed that structure consists of three parts: beginning, middle and end. We have studied poetics and rhetoric, and many speeches do not have this even in its most basic form. Then, when I moved on to studying hero archetypes, I thought, “Okay, the performer is the hero, he’s on stage, he’s the star of the show.” It's easy to feel like a star when giving a presentation.

I immediately realized that it doesn't work that way. If I have an idea, I can share it, but if you don’t understand it, if it doesn’t touch you, then this idea will disappear and the world will never change. Therefore, in reality, the speaker is not the hero; the hero of our idea is the audience. If you look at Joseph Campbell's hero's journey, it was only at the beginning that there were really interesting ideas. There is a relatable hero in the mundane world who feels the call to adventure. And the world seems to lose harmony. At first the hero resists, he’s like, “I’m not sure I want to get involved in this.” And then a mentor comes and helps him to leave the ordinary world and enter a special world.

And this is the role of the speaker - to be a mentor. You are not Luke Skywalker, you are Yoda. You are the one who truly helps the audience move from the initial state to your new and special idea. And that is the power of history. The simplest structure in the story is three parts. You have a compelling hero who has a desire, who faces an obstacle and is ultimately transformed— that's the basic structure. But that was until I came across Gustav Freytag's pyramid: he invented this figure in 1863. He was a German playwright... he was a German playwright and he believed in a five-part structure, which has an exposition, a plot, a climax, a resolution, and an ending where the story's problem is revealed or resolved.

I like this figure. Let's talk about figures. There is an arc in history, and an arc is a figure. We say that classical music is well composed. So I thought, "If presentations had a shape, what would it be?" and “How did the greatest orators use this figure, and did they use it at all?” I will never forget it, it was Saturday morning. After all this research - two years of research - I drew a figure. And I was like, “Oh my god, if this figure exists, then I could take two completely different speeches and superimpose it on them and it would be true.” I took the obvious: I took Martin Luther King’s “I Have a Dream” speech and Steve Jobs’s speech at the presentation of the iPhone in 2007.

I put a shape on them and it worked. I sat in my office, completely stunned. I even cried a little: “This is just a gift from above.” And here it is, here is the figure of a magnificent presentation. Is n't it wonderful? (Sobbing) (Laughter) I cried. I want to take you through it, it's quite amazing. There is a beginning, a middle and an end, and I want to walk you through it all. Because great speakers... I've gone through speeches and all that... I can really put on a figure. Even the Gettysburg Address fits it. At the beginning of any presentation you need to show what you have. You know, "this is the status quo, this is what's happening." And then you need to compare that to what could have been.

You need to make this difference as big as possible, because there is the ordinariness of the status quo, and you need to show the grandeur of your idea in contrast. For example: “There is the past, there is the present, but look at our future.” "Here's a problem, but look how it disappears." "Here is an obstacle, let's destroy it." You need to really emphasize this difference. It works like a cliffhanger in a movie. And then the audience should suddenly be wondering about what you just laid out: “Wow, do I want to agree and come to terms with this or not?” And for the rest of the presentation, they should support this idea.

In the middle, one can move back and forth and oscillate between what is and what could be, what is and what could be. You are trying to make the status quo and the norm unattractive and want to entice the audience with what could be in the future if your idea were accepted. People will resist your path to changing the world. They won't catch fire: they can love the world as it is. You will encounter resistance. So you have to move back and forth. It's like swimming. When you are sailing against the wind and the wind is resisting you need to steer the boat back and forth, back and forth. This way you can catch the wind.

You need to catch the resistance directed against you as you swim. What's interesting is that if you catch the wind correctly and set your sail correctly, your boat will actually go faster than the wind itself. This is a physical phenomenon. When it comes to speaking up, having them disagree with what is and what could be will actually get them on board with your idea faster than if you didn't. After you've wavered between what is and what could be, the final turning point is the call to action, which should be in any presentation, but at the very end. You need to describe the world as a new hope. “This is the kind of utopia that will arise if my idea is accepted.” "This is what the world will look like when we come together and solve this serious problem." You need to use this as an ending in a very poetic and dramatic way.

What's interesting is that when I finished, I thought, "You know what? I can use this for analysis." I actually transcribed speeches and worked out how they fit this pattern. I want to show some of them today. And I want to start with the people I took on first. Here is Mr. Jobs, who completely changed the world. It has changed the world of personal computers, the music industry, and is now on its way to changing the mobile device industry. He definitely changed the world. And here is the form of his speech in 2007, when he released his iPhone. It's a 90-minute speech, you can see how he starts with what is, moves back and forth, and ends with what could be.

I want to take a closer look at this: the white line is where he speaks, his speech. The next colored line you'll see appear is where it breaks in the video. This way he adds variety by inserting his own video. So he doesn't do all the talking himself. These lines are clearly shown here. Towards the end you will see a blue line. This is a guest speaker. And this is where things get interesting: the checkmarks here are where he made everyone laugh. And every tick here is where he was applauded. The audience is physically involved in the presentation, they physically respond to what he says, and that's actually amazing because then you can be sure that you have the audience.

He begins with what could have been: “I have been looking forward to this day for two and a half years.” He's launching a product he's known about for a couple of years. So this product is not new to him. But look at what he does: he admires. He admires his own product. He himself admires more than the audience laughs or applauds. It's like he's saying, 'Isn't it cool? "Is n't it wonderful?" He models for the audience the emotions he wants them to feel. Basically , he forces them to feel a certain way. Here he begins with what could have been: “Every now and then a revolutionary product comes along and changes everything.” He starts to go into detail and talks about his new product.

At first he doesn't turn on the phone. And you can see that the line is mostly white up to this point, and it's oscillating between, "Here's this new phone, and here are the competitors that suck. Here's this new phone, and here are the crappy competitors." And then, at that moment, his moment of glory - and that is what we will always remember. He turns on the phone. The audience sees scrolling for the first time, you can hear the oxygen leaving the room. They gasped in amazement. This way he creates a moment that they will remember forever. If you move the model, you can see the blue color where the guest speakers enter, and the line breaks off towards the bottom right corner.

It's because his remote control is broken. He wants to keep the excitement alive and tells a story from his personal life right at the point where technology failed. He is a master communicator and he tells a story to keep his audience engaged. At the top right he ends with new hope. He leaves them with the promise that Apple will continue to create revolutionary products. And he says, "There's an old Wayne Gretzky quote that I really love: 'I skate to where the puck is going to be, not where it's been.' We've tried to follow this from the very beginning at Apple and we always will." And he ends with a new utopia.

Now let's look at Mr. King. He was a brilliant strategist and preacher who fought for equality throughout his life. And here is the form of his speech: “I have a dream.” You see, he starts with what is, moves from what is to what could be, and ends with a very poetic ideal, we all know that famous part. I'll enlarge this part a little and stretch it out for you. Here I have placed a transcript of the entire speech. I know you can't read this. But at the end of each line I made a break because he would take a breath and stop. A Southern Baptist preacher, most people had never heard anything like him before, so his pace and rhythm of speech were unfamiliar to people.

I want to cover these lines with text with a stripe because I'm using it here for information. Let's go over how he actually spoke to people. The blue stripes here would indicate that he used the oratorical technique of repetition. He repeated himself, he used the same words and phrases so that people could remember and reproduce them. But he also used metaphors and imagery. It was a way to take very complex ideas and make them memorable and informative so that people would understand them. He actually created almost pictures with his words so that they could illustrate what he was saying. He also used many famous songs and Bible quotes.

You see only the beginning. He also made many political references to the promises that were made to the people. If you look at the first time he spoke about what is, at the very end of what is, for the first time people really applauded and roared loudly. So, at the end of it all, he said, "America gave black people a bad check that came back marked 'insufficient funds.'" Everyone knows what it's like to have no money in your account. And he used a metaphor that is very close to people. But for the first time they really caught fire and really shouted at the words: “And we have come to cash this check, a check that will give us the treasures of freedom and the guarantees of justice.” Then they really applauded.

Then he compared what we have now with what could be. If you move a little further into this pattern, you will see it moving back and forth at a more frantic pace. And then he starts walking back and forth, back and forth. The audience was already on edge by then. They were all excited, so you can use this to keep them excited. He says: "I have a dream that one day this nation will rise up and live up to its creed." "We hold to these truths to be an example that men are created equal." He uses a little orange text to remind them of the promise made to him by politicians and this country. Then he goes back and forth, "I have a dream that one day, I have a dream that one day, I have a dream that one day," and at the end it gets very interesting because he uses—look at the four shades of green, there's a lot of blue here, so he used a lot of repetition, he has a high level of repetition.

And green means a high frequency of songs and biblical texts. So, the first batch of green is the actual texts from the Book of Prophet Isaiah. The second batch of green is "My country, it's about you." It's a famous song that was especially important to black people at the time because it was a song where they changed the words to a cry of despair, saying that promises were not kept. And the third batch of green is an excerpt from the song “My Country, It’s About You.” And the fourth is a spiritual song of African Americans. "Finally free! Finally free! Thank you, Lord, I am finally free! He, in essence, reached into the depths of the listeners' souls.

He quoted sacred texts, and that's important. He selected excerpts from songs they sang together to protest against the breaking of the law, and he used all of this as a means of connecting and relating to the audience. In the end, he paints a picture of new hope, using that very thing within them that they already considered hidden. He was a great man and he had a great dream. There are a lot of people sitting here, and you all have really big dreams. There are truly great ideas within you that you need to share. But you know, we are facing difficulties. Changing the world is not easy – it is hard work.

You know, he was... his house was bombed, they stuck a box cutter into it. In the end, he lost his life because he cared. But many of us won't have to make such sacrifices. What happens, though, is that it's a bit like the basic structure of a story. Life can be like this. You know, you are all nice people, you have desire, you face obstacles, and that's where we stop. We all do this: “I had an idea, but I’m not going to share it. She's already been rejected once." You know, we sabotage our own ideas, we just back away and back away from obstacles, instead of allowing difficulties to change us and go forward and implement this idea.

And you know, if everyone... if I can do it, then everyone can. I grew up in an economically and emotionally impoverished environment. The first time I went to camp with my sister, I was abused. This was not the first case of violence, but it was the most aggressive. And my mom and dad... they married each other three times. (Mumbling) Yes, it was exciting, and when they weren't fighting, they were helping the alcoholics who lived with us sober up because they were both sober. My mother left us when I was 16. I looked after the house and my brothers and sisters. And I got married, I met a man.

Fell in love. I studied at college for a year. I did everything a single, vibrant young woman should do: I got married when I was 18. And you know what? I knew, I knew that I was born for something more. And at that moment in my life I had a choice. I could have let it all crush me, let all my ideas die inside me. I could say that life is too complicated to change the world. It's just too heavy. But I chose a different story for my life. (Laughter) Don't know which one? I think there are people in this room... you have these little baking spices and you think, "You know, it's not that important. “ I can’t change the whole world.” But you know, you can change your world.

You can change your life. You can change the world under your control, you can change your environment. I want to encourage you to do this. Because you know what? The future is not a place where we end up. This is the place we need to create. Thank you. Be healthy. (Applause)

Consultant Explains the Pyramid Principle

Ah, the notorious pyramid principle. You may love it, hate it, or perhaps you've never even heard of it, but there's a more than likely chance you've already seen it used in a presentation. In this video, I'll discuss what the pyramid principle is, how it's used in major consulting firms, and why it's so useful. (Upbeat music) Simply put, the pyramid principle is just a structured form of communication where you start with the main point and then move through the supporting details of that main point. So, for example, let's say you asked your friend who their favorite basketball player is. She might say something like: I like players who can play in different positions, but who can also score a lot of points and be team leaders.

So, I really like LeBron James. Now, observe the structure of this response. That's reason number one - she likes players who can play in different positions - reason number two - she likes players who can score a lot of points - and reason number three - she likes players who can be team leaders. And then the answer comes right at the end. And this is a perfectly normal and acceptable way to answer a question. But let's say she used the pyramid principle, in which case she might say something like, "My favorite player is LeBron James because he can play in different positions, scores a lot of points, and is a team leader." So, did you notice the difference between the two?

In the second example, she gets straight to the point and then follows through with her reasoning to that main point. And that makes everything much easier for me, as a listener, because when I know she 's talking about LeBron James, it's much easier to follow her reasoning. Now, let's take this example a step further and say that she's going to map this out for you on paper. But that's not all; She will add a few more details to her argument. So, we arrive at the main point: LeBron James is your favorite player, after the three reasons we stated earlier. And now we have some details for those reasons.

And if you didn't already know, this is where the information resembles a pyramid, with the main point at the top and the details organized logically and structurally below. But there's something much more important happening here. Each box is intended to capture the main point of all the boxes below it. So, for example, this box here provides a nice summary statement for the two below it. And of course, if you look at our top box, you'll see a summary of the entire pyramid. At this point, it's worth pausing to note that the whole idea of ​​the pyramid principle came from a woman named Barbara Minto, who was a consultant at McKinsey in the 1960s.

So, if you really enjoy studying logical structure and communication, her book is a great read. It's called the "Pyramid Principle," and we'll certainly include a link to it in the description below. Okay, so we put our pyramid in place. Now let's make this a little more practical. Let's say your friend now wants to convey her point of view, so she'll give a full presentation about it. All she needs to do is organize these ideas onto her own slides to form the outline of the presentation, also called a storyboard. Notice how her first slide presents the main idea in summary, and then she goes into detail in the following slides.

This is the pyramid principle in action, and it's exactly how leading consulting firms apply it in their client presentations. There are so many advantages to this approach, but one of them is that it is more efficient. If your friend had waited until the end to tell you that her favorite player is LeBron James, your brain would have had to go back and think about the different reasons she had already given you and try to evaluate each reason after the fact. But if she gives you the answer beforehand, you can evaluate each reason she presents and then decide if it's something you agree with. In a real presentation setting, this approach has the added benefit of saving time because if, for example, you tell an executive your main point at the beginning, you can spend your time on the parts of that main point with which he or she disagrees. instead of having to watch each part of the presentation just to figure out the main point at the end.

It 's also much more flexible. Since the first slide contains the main idea, she could simply present that slide and you would understand what she is trying to tell you. Or, if she had more time, she could present the first slide, then the three main supporting points, and that would be it. So, of course, if she had unlimited time, she could give the full presentation with all the details. But in each of these scenarios, the overall message remains unchanged. That's because you have more details. So, one final reason is that this makes the argument easy to follow. The goal of your presentation is to make it as easy as possible for your audience to understand your main message.

And the pyramid principle helps someone easily see what your main point is and how you arrived at each of your conclusions. In the world of consulting, it's important to back up all your claims, and the pyramid principle provides a structured way to do that. So there you have it: a brief explanation of the pyramid principle.
